page_title: Fallow — Smart Daily Time Allocation & To-Do Planner
page_meta_description: A smart to-do planner that splits your daily time across tasks with the Zenith Gradient algorithm — balancing effort, enjoyment, and flow across the hours you actually have.
seo_image_alt: Fallow — a to-do app that finds the mathematically optimal way to spend your day
about_hook_title: A to-do app that does calculus so you don't have to
about_hook_body: Every productive day poses the same question: you have more tasks than hours — how should you split your time to get the most out of the day? Fallow doesn't guess and doesn't split evenly. It models each task's productivity curve and solves for the time allocation with the highest average productivity per task, summed across your day — within the hours you have and the mental and physical energy you can actually sustain.
about_how_body_1: Productivity over time isn't flat. On any task you start at some initial level, ramp up as you get into the zone, peak at flow state, then decay as you tire. Fallow describes that curve with three things you feel intuitively: how demanding the task is (effort), how much you like doing it (enjoyment), and how long it takes you to get going (time to flow).
about_how_body_2: Enjoyable, low-effort tasks start productive right away; hard, unpleasant ones start slow but peak higher. Every task also has a mathematically optimal stopping point beyond which your average productivity on it falls. The better Fallow knows your flow times, the closer the point it plans for sits to 1.52–1.79 times the time-to-flow; the less sure it is, the earlier it stops. Fallow plans in 15-minute blocks and never pushes a task past that point.
about_different_body_1: Fallow doesn't guess the allocation: greedy marginal analysis over 15-minute block values, with an exhaustive search over which tasks deserve any time at all once context-switch costs are charged. When only your hours have to be respected, that search returns the exact optimum for up to 12 tasks, and past that whenever your day, list and switch cost together keep it bounded; once the cognitive and physical pools bind as well, it reaches the optimum on about 94% of days and lands within a few per cent on the rest. It then reports the Fallow Gain — how much better the optimized plan is than an equal split.
about_different_body_2: A dual energy-pool model tracks cognitive and physical capacity separately, so a day can't book more hard thinking than you have head for — and the suggested run order alternates the two systems instead of burning one down. The model also personalizes itself: log how long it took you to reach flow, and a least-squares fit tunes its constants to you.
about_energy_post: takes it further — breaks and quitting time emerge from the math.
about_faq_a1: Yes. Fallow is free and open source — the full model, including every formula and derivation, is documented publicly.
about_faq_a1_support: If it helps you, you can support development and
about_faq_a2: Entirely on your device, in your browser's local database (IndexedDB). Your tasks never leave your machine and no account is required.
about_faq_q3: What is the Zenith Gradient Algorithm?
about_faq_a3: An approach to daily time allocation that models each task's productivity as a curve that rises to flow state and then decays, and allocates your day by marginal value — every next block of time goes to the task where it currently counts most. It originated in the article "How to Over-Engineer a To-Do App"; Fallow extends it with corrected math, energy pools, and context-switch costs.
header_tagline: Splits your daily time budget so each extra minute goes to the task where it counts most — accounting for flow ramp-up, context-switch costs, and your cognitive and physical capacity, and never pushing a task past its point of diminishing returns.
list_empty_hint: Add a task to begin tracking
task_run_order_tooltip: Suggested run order — alternates cognitive and physical work so the resting energy system recovers
task_nature_cognitive_description: Cognitive task — mental difficulty dominates, draws on the cognitive capacity pool
task_nature_physical_description: Physical task — physical difficulty dominates, draws on the physical capacity pool
task_nature_hybrid_description: Hybrid task — balanced mental and physical demands, draws on both capacity pools
task_derived_tooltip: What the Fallow model derived from your sliders: true effort E (1–5), time to reach flow state ϕ, and the optimal stopping time beyond which average productivity declines. The better Fallow knows your flow times, the closer that time sits to 1.52–1.79×ϕ; the less sure it is, the earlier it stops — for a task that is productive from the first minute, even before ϕ.
task_flow_badge_tooltip: Measured minutes-to-flow you logged for this task — data points like this personalize the model's c₁,c₂,c₃ constants (least-squares fit)
task_allocation_tooltip: Suggested time allocation for today, and the task's priority score (intrinsic value × 10) that drives it
next_up_tooltip: Where to pick up now: first in the run order re-planned from the hours you have logged today. The #1 badge in the list below is the whole-day plan's order and stays the answer it was this morning. It never tells you to stop for the day — the Energy Lab's stop advisor is what prices that.
task_remaining_tooltip: Of the {left} still unspent today, this is what the model would spend on this task now — re-planned from the hours you have logged, so a task you already worked no longer collects its start-up bonus and one past its stopping time is offered nothing. It is time to spend ON TOP of what you have done. Your whole-day plan is a separate reading and does not change as you work.
task_log_flow_tooltip: Log how many minutes it took to get into flow — measured data points personalize the model's c₁,c₂,c₃ constants
budget_unplanned: {hours}h left unplanned — capped by optimal stopping times & capacity pools
budget_unplanned_title: The plan deliberately stops short of your budget: each task is capped at its own optimal stopping time (where its average productivity peaks, hedged for how well Fallow knows your flow times) and by your cognitive/physical capacity pools. The unused hours are recovery time, not lost time.
budget_cognitive_hint: Intense mental work you sustain per day (~4h)
budget_physical_hint: Intense physical work you sustain per day (~6h)
budget_model_tooltip: The model's flow-state constants (c₁, c₂, c₃) are a ridge least-squares fit of your measured time-to-flow data, anchored to the article's defaults.
budget_delete_log_title: Remove this data point — the model refits without it
budget_reset_confirm: Delete all {count} logs and revert to defaults?
budget_reset_title: Delete all flow logs — the constants are always derived from the logs (never stored), so the model reverts to the article defaults
day_timeline_legend: A filled bar reached flow, a short one stopped before it, and the gaps are the switch cost.
momentum_tooltip: Average enjoyment minus difficulty across your remaining tasks — completed ones drop out. Upward = the work ahead is motivating, Reset Reqd = it drains more than it rewards.
model_status_personalized: Model personalized from {count} time-to-flow logs (⚡) — recent ones count most, blended with the defaults
model_status_personalized_one: Model personalized from 1 time-to-flow log (⚡) — blended with the defaults, sharpens as you log more
model_status_implausible: Your {count} flow logs produced an implausible fit (predicted flow times over 16h) — using default constants. Check the logs below for mistakes.
model_status_implausible_one: Your 1 flow log produced an implausible fit (predicted flow times over 16h) — using default constants. Check the logs below for mistakes.
model_status_default: Model uses default constants — log time-to-flow (⚡) on tasks to start personalizing
model_status_pending: {count} ⚡ logged today — they re-time your model from tomorrow, so today's plan holds
model_status_pending_one: 1 ⚡ logged today — it re-times your model from tomorrow, so today's plan holds
banner_future_body: tasks and budget you set here are saved to {date} — open it on that day to work the plan.
banner_past_body: you can still check tasks on or off (forgot one before midnight? fix it here — changes are saved), but adding or editing tasks is only possible on today.
metric_zenith_gain_desc: Productivity improvement from Fallow optimization vs. a naive equal split of the same hours into the same 15-minute blocks. The split spreads over as many tasks as the day can fit and pays only for the switches it makes, so both plans face the same constraints.
metric_yield_index_desc: Did you complete the highest-priority tasks? Compares your completed work against the optimal selection.
metric_completion_rate_desc: Priority-weighted progress. High-value tasks contribute more to this percentage than low-priority ones.
metric_flow_coverage_desc: Tasks that reach flow state (allocated time ≥ ϕ). Low coverage means too many tasks for budget — drop tasks or add hours.
metric_human_capacity_desc: {type} limit ({hours}h/day, configurable in Time Budget). The allocator enforces these pools, so suggested plans stay ≤100% — this shows how much of your sustainable capacity the plan uses.
metric_human_capacity_desc_none: How much of your sustainable capacity the plan uses. With no tasks yet, neither pool binds — add a task and this names the one that does (both are configurable in Time Budget).
metric_capacity_left_desc: The share of your {type} pool ({hours}h/day, configurable in Time Budget) that today's logged hours have not spent — {percent}% of it is gone. An hour counts at the task's difficulty, so an hour on a 2/10 task spends 12 minutes of the pool, not an hour. Human Capacity judges the day as planned and the allocator holds that at ≤100%; this counts the hours you actually worked, so it can go past.
metric_capacity_left_desc_none: What today's logged hours have left of your capacity pools. It reads once a session is rated (🪫) against a pool that has hours in it — the pool those hours load hardest, and how much of it is gone.
metric_time_scarcity_desc: How stretched is your time budget? Higher values mean too many tasks for the hours available.
metric_bottleneck_desc: Of the work still ahead, the task drawing most on your {type} pool — the pool what is left loads hardest. Human Capacity judges the day as planned, so once you finish something the two can name different pools. It is the biggest single term in that pool's saturation: demand × planned hours. Naming a task is not a verdict on it; whether the pool is over-drawn is Human Capacity's reading.
metric_bottleneck_desc_none: The task drawing most on whichever capacity pool binds your day. Nothing left draws on it — a finished plan, no hours yet, or remaining work that only loads the other system.
metric_longest_warm_up_desc: Of the work still ahead, {task} takes the longest to reach flow state — ϕ, the warm-up the model derives from its difficulty and enjoyment. Amber when today's plan funds fewer hours than that, so the warm-up never pays off.
metric_longest_warm_up_desc_none: How long the slowest of your remaining tasks takes to reach flow state (ϕ). Nothing left to warm up.
metric_burnout_risk_desc: Your planned day simulated through the energy model: each task drains the cognitive and physical reservoirs by its demand and duration (drain and recovery rates come from your own calibration logs). Risk is how depleted the most-drained reservoir ends the day — hours you intend beyond the plan are simulated as extra work, and yesterday's logged work carries into this morning's starting energy.
metric_cognitive_load_desc: Share of your time budget taken by cognitive work, weighted by each task's mental difficulty. 8h of medium-difficulty mental work in an 8h day reads 50%.
metric_physical_load_desc: Share of your time budget taken by physical work, weighted by each task's physical difficulty. 8h of medium-difficulty physical work in an 8h day reads 50%.
metric_energy_balance_desc: Distribution of Cognitive vs physical work. Alternating types extends total productive hours.
metric_schedule_integrity_desc: Share of the plan's committed time that is productive work rather than context-switch overhead. One long session ≈ 100%; many small sessions drive it down.
metric_friction_index_desc: Size of the gap between difficulty and enjoyment, averaged over your allocated hours and measured against the largest gap there is (9, on the 1–10 scales). A whole day running 4 points of difficulty past its enjoyment reads 44%, not the 100% a share-of-time reading would give. 100% = every planned hour is enjoyment-1 work at difficulty 10, which a task rated 8 in both dimensions reaches too.
metric_deep_work_desc: Share of your time budget in sustained-focus work, ramped by mental difficulty: nothing counts below 5, half an hour of credit at 7, the whole hour from 9 up. A quarter to 60% of the day is the shape to aim for — past that, Burnout Risk owns the verdict.
metric_quick_wins_desc: Count of easy, enjoyable tasks available for momentum building and motivation boosts.
metric_grind_density_desc: Share of today's funded tasks where difficulty exceeds enjoyment. High values signal willpower drain.
metric_sustainable_work_desc: Share of the hours the plan actually allocates that go to tasks whose enjoyment covers their difficulty (both dimensions together). Unbooked time and switch overhead are not counted against you. Higher = more energizing workday.
metric_recovery_ratio_desc: Easy tasks (≤4) per hard tasks (≥7). Aim for 1:2 or 1:3 ratio for ultradian rhythm recovery.
metric_day_profile_desc: Your day's character, weighted by the hours the plan books: difficulty across both dimensions against enjoyment. Flow Zone = challenging and engaging, Grind Mode = demanding work, Cruise = light and enjoyable, Routine = low-key tasks.
metric_avg_physical_desc: Average physical difficulty across all tasks.
metric_avg_mental_desc: Average mental/cognitive difficulty across all tasks.
metric_avg_enjoyment_desc: Average enjoyment across all tasks. Higher values indicate more engaging work.

advice_switch_cost_none: At {declared} a switch, this plan pays for no switching.

advice_unfunded_one: 1 task gets no hours in this plan.

ana_load_trend_hint: Burnout Risk and the two Loads per day. History solves the plan more cheaply than the dashboard does, so a single day can sit a few points off.

ana_day_profiles_hint: Character of your active days: challenging & engaging (Flow), demanding (Grind), light & fun (Cruise), or low-key (Routine)
ana_adherence_hint: How closely your logged work (🪫) tracked each planner's suggested day — compared as composition (which tasks got the time), not total hours.
ana_adherence_empty: Needs finished days with 🪫 drain logs. Log worked minutes on your tasks and check back.

ana_adherence_verdict_classic: Your days track the classic plan more closely.

ana_model_trend_aria: {label} over the last {count} recorded days: {from} to {to}

ana_logs_empty: No measurements logged in this range.
energy_meta_description: Day-value scheduler: energy reservoirs drain as you work and recover as you rest; breaks and quitting time emerge from the math.
energy_intro_1: A different engine than the main page: instead of maximizing each task's average productivity, this scheduler maximizes
energy_intro_2: — your total output, worth less on each task the longer you stay on it, priced against what your free time and the energy you have left at the end of the day are worth to you. Two energy reservoirs (cognitive and physical) drain while you work and recover while you rest, and warm-up restarts every time you switch — so rest breaks, task order, and your quitting time all
energy_intro_3: instead of being rules. It shares the task list with the main page — edits here save to today's session.
energy_all_done_hint: The planner needs an open task — un-check one below or add a new one.
energy_stop_advisor_hint: Prices your best next work session from today's 🪫 work logs, under the current parameters. Worth more per hour than your free time — keep going; worth less — a good place to stop. Log sessions as you finish them to keep this honest.
energy_stop_continue_detail: Your next session — {duration} of {task} — is worth ≈ {value}/h, above the {free}/h your free time is worth to you.
energy_stop_stop_detail: Even the best next session — {duration} of {task} at ≈ {value}/h — is worth less than the {free}/h your free time is worth to you.
energy_stop_window_full: No whole work session fits in what's left of your day window.
energy_set_window: Set a day window above 0 hours.
energy_chart_aria: Energy levels and output rate over the day
energy_nothing_scheduled: Nothing scheduled — with the current parameters, free time is worth more than any task's output. Lower the free-time value or check your day window.
energy_vs_classic: Day value vs the classic plan, judged by this model
energy_vs_classic_title: The classic allocator's plan for the same tasks and window, scored by this model's own objective — output after diminishing returns, plus what the day's free time and leftover energy are worth. Not raw output, which is the one thing the schedule above was not chosen to maximize. It is the only reading here that uses your switch cost and capacity pools — this engine has neither — so editing those on the main page moves this percentage without changing the schedule above.
energy_curve_desc: Every window is re-solved by the same optimizer that built your plan, then scored on one common horizon — so the hours compare with each other and not just with themselves.
energy_curve_stale: Your day has changed since this was calculated.
energy_curve_unrun: No window has been priced for this day yet.
energy_curve_recommendation: Past {hours} another hour of your day adds nothing — it buys less than the free time it costs. That window books {work} of work.
energy_curve_no_crossing: Out to the {max} it checked, another hour of your day is still worth more than the free time it costs — this model would use every hour you give it.
energy_curve_no_work: At this price on your free time, no day window is worth working — out to the {max} it checked, the model books nothing at any length.
energy_curve_no_crossing_hint: Your free time is priced at {value} output an hour, and the curve above already charges it. That price is what sets the length of your day here, and the stopping calibration below fits it from how your own days end.
energy_curve_legend_value: What another hour of window adds, after paying for your free time
energy_curve_legend_now_offscale: Your window now is {hours}, past the {max} checked here
energy_curve_chart_aria: What each extra hour of the day window adds to the day's value after the free time it costs, over day windows up to {max}. It never rises as the window grows.
energy_curve_chart_aria_recommended: The last window where it is still above zero is the suggested one, at {hours}.
energy_reset_defaults_title: Restore all model parameters to their defaults
energy_apply_fits_title: Set the recovery rate, the two drain rates and the free-time value to what your own ☕/🪫 logs fit — in the one order the model admits: recovery first, then drain, then free-time value
energy_day_window_hint: The same hours as the main page's Available Hours — one budget for both planners, so changing it here changes it there
energy_cognitive_drain_hint: How fast deep mental work empties the mind tank (a level from 1 = full to 0 = empty). At 0.35/h, flat-out thinking halves it in about 2 hours; 0.7/h halves it in 1 hour, 2/h in 20 minutes, 0.15/h in 5½. Your 🪫 Mind ratings fit this number for you.
energy_physical_drain_hint: How fast physically hard work empties the body tank (a level from 1 = full to 0 = empty). At 0.3/h, flat-out effort halves it in about 2½ hours; 0.6/h halves it in 1¼. Your 🪫 Body ratings fit this number for you.
energy_recovery_rate_hint: How fast an idle tank refills. At 0.7/h, one hour of rest takes you from half energy back to about 83%; at 0.1/h you only reach 57%, at 2/h about 97%. Your ☕ before/after rest pairs fit this number for you.
energy_free_time_value_hint: What an hour NOT worked is worth to you, in the same output units the plan measures work in — the lever that makes the plan stop instead of filling the whole day. On a 12-hour window it roughly moves the plan from all 12 hours of work at 0.2, to 11.25 at 0.5, to 10.5 at 0.8, to 6 at 1.0, to none at 1.5.
energy_evening_energy_hint: What ending the day with FULL tanks is worth, in output units — counted in proportion to how full the two tanks actually end up. At 1.5 that is worth about three free hours (at a free-time value of 0.5), so the plan won't spend you down to empty. 0 means the evening's state doesn't count at all.
energy_satiety_hint: Diminishing returns for piling more of the day onto the same task — after this many good sessions' worth of output, extra output on it counts half. 1× satiates after one good session, 0.5× twice as fast, 3× barely at all. 0 turns it off (one task can then win the whole day).
energy_micro_recovery_hint: Share of recovery that stays active even while working flat out (micro-pauses between efforts). It sets the floor a maximum-demand task drains toward instead of zero: 5% ≈ a 13–15% floor, 20% ≈ 40%, 30% ≈ half a tank — at which point you can't really run yourself down. 0 turns it off.
energy_log_drain_tooltip: After working on this task, rate how drained you feel (mind and body, 0–10) — the ratings calibrate the drain rates to you. Applying a fit re-plans the whole window from scratch, so the payoff lands on your next session, not the rest of today
energy_drain_mind_title: How mentally drained you feel now: 0 = fresh, 10 = completely spent
energy_drain_body_title: How physically drained you feel now: 0 = fresh, 10 = completely spent
energy_calibration_hint: Fits the two drain rates to your 🪫 end-of-session ratings (anchored to the defaults — every rating nudges them further). The fit conditions on the current recovery settings, which is why Apply my fits sets recovery first.
energy_calibration_empty: No ratings yet. After a session on a task, hit 🪫 on it and rate how drained your mind and body feel — a few ratings personalize the drain rates.
energy_drain_pending_one: 1 rating logged today, counted from tomorrow
energy_drain_pending: {count} ratings logged today, counted from tomorrow
energy_edit_drain_log_title: Re-open this session in the editor — each rating is one session, so correct it here rather than logging it again
energy_delete_drain_log_title: Remove this rating from the calibration
energy_reset_drain_title: Delete every drain rating — the calibration reverts to the defaults
energy_recovery_calibration_hint: Fits the recovery rate to your ☕ rest pairs — rate mind and body before and after a break. During rest, drain fades independently of the drain rates, so a few pairs pin down recovery on its own; the drain calibration then builds on it.
energy_recovery_calibration_empty: No rest pairs yet. Before a break, note how drained mind and body feel (0–10); rate them again afterwards — a few pairs personalize the recovery rate. If you recover fast, short breaks carry the most signal.
energy_rest_pending_one: 1 break logged today, counted from tomorrow
energy_rest_pending: {count} breaks logged today, counted from tomorrow
energy_stop_calibration_hint: Fits the free-time value to when you actually stop working: each past day's 🪫 worked minutes are compared against the work still open at the end of it — stopping while worthwhile work was left means leisure is worth more to you than the model assumed. A day you checked everything off forwent nothing, so it is skipped. This fit conditions on recovery and drain, so Apply my fits sets it last.
energy_stop_calibration_empty: No finished days yet. Log 🪫 drain ratings (with worked minutes) on your tasks; every past day with ratings becomes one stop observation here.
energy_stop_calibration_censored: No informative days yet — days worked to the window's edge (or barely at all), days that ended with every task checked off, and days that look cut short mid-session (an interruption, not a chosen stop), reveal only an inequality, not an indifference point.

privacy_controller_body: Responsible for the data processing on this website (full contact details in the imprint):
privacy_local_heading: Your data stays in your browser
privacy_local_body: Everything you enter into Fallow — tasks, daily sessions, ratings, calibration data and model settings — is stored exclusively on your own device (IndexedDB and localStorage in your browser). This content is never transmitted to us or to any server, and there are no user accounts. If you clear your browser data, it is gone. The only data that does leave your browser are the four display-preference cookies described in the next section, which your browser sends with every request. This local storage is strictly necessary to provide the app and therefore requires no consent (§ 25 (2) TDDDG).
privacy_cookies_body: Fallow sets four first-party cookies (path /), all of them display preferences — no identifier, no tracking, nothing about your tasks. The server reads them on every request so the very first paint already uses your theme and language: "theme" holds the selected colour theme (one year), "scenerySeed" a random number that varies the animated background (one year; the server generates it on your first visit, before you change anything), "sceneryMotion" whether background animation is paused (one year) and "PARAGLIDE_LOCALE" the interface language (about 13 months). They are strictly necessary for a service you explicitly requested, so no consent is required (§ 25 (2) TDDDG); the legal basis for the processing is our legitimate interest in rendering the page correctly on the first request (Art. 6 (1) (f) GDPR). You can delete them in your browser at any time — Fallow then falls back to its defaults.
privacy_hosting_body: This website is hosted by Vercel Inc., 440 N Barranca Ave #4133, Covina, CA 91723, USA. When you visit it, Vercel processes the data your browser transmits with each request — in particular your IP address, date and time, the requested page, browser and operating system — in server logs to deliver the site and to ensure its stability and security. The legal basis is our legitimate interest in the reliable operation of the site (Art. 6 (1) (f) GDPR).
privacy_analytics_body: We use Vercel Web Analytics to measure how this site is used in aggregate (page views, referrer, browser and device type, country/region derived from the IP address). The tool sets no cookies and stores nothing on your device. Visitors are counted via a hash derived from the incoming request; it is automatically discarded after 24 hours and cannot track you across other websites. The legal basis is our legitimate interest in privacy-friendly reach measurement (Art. 6 (1) (f) GDPR).
privacy_speed_body: We also use Vercel Speed Insights to collect anonymized loading-performance metrics (Core Web Vitals) for visited pages. It sets no cookies and builds no visitor profiles. The legal basis is our legitimate interest in keeping the site fast and working (Art. 6 (1) (f) GDPR).
privacy_transfer_body: Vercel Inc. is based in the USA. Vercel is certified under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework (DPF); in addition, Vercel's data processing agreement, which includes the EU Standard Contractual Clauses, applies. An adequate level of data protection is therefore ensured for these transfers (Art. 45, 46 GDPR).
privacy_rights_body: You have the right of access (Art. 15 GDPR) and the rights to rectification (Art. 16), erasure (Art. 17), restriction of processing (Art. 18), data portability (Art. 20) and — for processing based on legitimate interest — objection (Art. 21 GDPR). You also have the right to lodge a complaint with a data protection supervisory authority. To exercise your rights, use the contact details in the imprint.
